transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 14:30 PST
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Jonah (CTO - CobaltPharma), Priya (SRE Lead), Alex (ML Eng)

Summary: deep dive on intermittent OOMs, CUDA timeouts, and KV-cache eviction/backpressure during mixed-batch production traffic. Goal: reproduce, root-cause, and agree on mitigations and next steps for a pilot.

Topics: eviction heuristics, batching/backpressure, quantization interactions, cudaMalloc fragmentation, watchdog timeout patterns, retry semantics and idempotency, VPC/on-prem constraints.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: All right thanks everyone for hopping on — let's do quick intros and then jump into the traces you sent.
[00:15] Jonah: Jonah here, quick recap — we've been seeing spikes where some requests slow to minutes, others hit soft oom or GPU watchdog reset. Happening at ~peak traffic windows with a mixed sequence length distribution.
[00:27] Maya: Got it. We looked through the traces you uploaded (link in chat). Top-level thing I saw was repeated CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT around the same time as kvcache_eviction bursts. Seems like eviction + prefetch is contending with compute for CUDA streams and memory.
[00:45] Priya: Yup, it's noisy — logs show 'CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED' and then a couple of device resets. Not every request fails, it's intermittent, usually when batch size ramps from 4->12 on high concurrency.
[01:05] Alex: We use a 7B quantized model (4-bit) with prefix caching. Our typical max_seq is 1024 but many requests are short (<=128). We tried raising max_batch_tokens to lower latency, but that seems to correlate with more OOMs.
[01:25] Maya: That matches a pattern — larger max_batch_tokens increases transient device allocs for KV prefetch and expanded attention workspace. With 4-bit quant, some kernels allocate temporary buffers that still go on GPU. Combined with fragmented cudaMalloc behavior it causes allocation failures under bursts.
[01:47] Samir: Quick clarifying question: are you running in Redwood Dedicated or Private on your VPC?
[01:52] Jonah: Private, on customer-managed AWS instances with our NVIDIA A10s. We run a handful of pods per node, one process per GPU, but we do run a small sidecar for metrics.
[02:07] Maya: A10s are fine, but fragmentation and CUDA context behavior differs by driver and libcudnn. Two things to check: enable cudaMallocAsync (driver >=11.3 required) and set pooled allocator flags; second, use kernel fallback that prefers memory-light attention kernels at long sequences.
[02:32] Priya: We have driver 11.8 and CUDA 11.8, should support cudaMallocAsync. We haven't enabled it across the fleet.
[02:40] Alex: One weird artifact — when kvcache eviction spikes, latency climbs and then the watchdog triggers; looks like eviction triggers synchronous cudaMalloc/free loops on the main thread.
[02:55] Maya: Right — our runtime's eviction implementation has a synchronous path for large evictions. If you evict N large prefixes at once that causes a short but high-volume allocation surge. We can toggle an async-eviction flag that spreads eviction over multiple micro-batches to avoid a single spike.
[03:12] Jonah: That would be great. But any tradeoffs? Would spreading eviction add latency to subsequent requests?
[03:20] Maya: Slight increase in tail for requests that would have hit the cache immediately after eviction, but overall avoids device resets and large hard OOMs. It's a classic backpressure smoothing tradeoff.
[03:33] Priya: We also saw cases where batching logic packs dissimilar seq-lengths. When a long sequence gets merged it expands token-dimension work and pushes memory. Is there guidance on bucketing vs dynamic batching?
[03:47] Samir: We typically recommend bucketing by seq-length for high variance workloads, with a small dynamic-batch cap to absorb short bursts. Example config: bucket thresholds [128, 512, 1024], max_batch_tokens per bucket tuned to keep peak alloc below 0.85*GPU_mem.
[04:05] Alex: Do you have tooling to compute expected allocs for a given batch composition?
[04:09] Maya: Yes — SE playbook has a token-cost model we can run against your request histogram. We'll include that in the deliverable.
[04:21] Jonah: Another datapoint: when we turned on quantization to 4-bit, we saw slightly different memory profiles depending on kernel selection — some kernels still need float32 temporaries and those blow up memory.
[04:36] Maya: Exactly. 4-bit reduces parameter storage, but some GEMM/workspace paths allocate FP32 intermediates. You can avoid the peak by using quantization-friendly kernels (we expose kernel profiles in the console). Also try limiting cudnn workspace size (CUDNN_WORKSPACE_LIMIT) to force memory-light algorithms.
[04:57] Priya: Can we get recommended env var set for our deployment to reduce fragmentation and prefetch pressure?
[05:03] Maya: Sure: enable CUDA_MALLOC_ASYNC=1, set MALLOC_TRIM_THRESHOLD_=131072 (if using glibc), set CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8 for deterministic allocs, and set REDWOOD_EVICTION_MODE=async_with_throttle. We'll provide exact snippets.
[05:24] Samir: Let's dig into the retry semantics — when a request fails with a soft OOM vs device reset, do you want the platform to retry automatically?
[05:33] Jonah: We want idempotent retries for short failures but not to hide systemic capacity issues. Currently retries are aggressive and we see duplicate downstream operations.
[05:43] Maya: We recommend a conservative retry policy: single fast retry for transient cudaMalloc failures (<200ms), exponential backoff for watchdog/device-reset cases with rate-limiting, and a dead-letter path for persistent failures. Also correlate retries with request idempotency header so you can dedupe application-side.
[06:02] Alex: How do you detect transient vs hard failure reliably in logs? Some CUDA errors are ambiguous.
[06:10] Maya: We classify by error codes and runtime signals: CUBLAS_STATUS_ALLOC_FAILED and cudaErrorMemoryAllocation are usually transient under fragmentation; CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_ADDRESS or device reset are hard. We combine with watchdog count in the agent to escalate.
[06:28] Priya: In our traces, a minority of failures had 'cudaFree pointer invalid' — could that be a use-after-free in our custom extension?
[06:36] Maya: Possibly. If you have custom ops we should run a memcheck and driver-level stacktrace. We'll add memory check steps in the playbook.
[06:46] Samir: Let's talk about preventing eviction storms — what's the recommended kvcache policy for a mixed short/long workload?
[06:54] Maya: Use LFU with aging plus a soft TTL on very large prefixes. That prevents repeated thrashing of large long-seq prefixes. Also cap total prefix bytes under a fraction of GPU memory, e.g., 0.4*GPU_mem, and set eviction_background_rate to smooth evictions.
[07:13] Alex: Could we offload cold prefixes to host RAM or NVMe to avoid re-fetch thrash?
[07:18] Maya: Yes, tiered caching: host RAM for warm prefixes and GPU for hot. Redwood supports async host-resident cache; the tradeoff is tail latency for misses. For your SLA (95% < 200ms) we recommend host-tier as a fallback only for very large cold prefixes.
[07:36] Jonah: On the networking side, since we're in VPC, we worry about k8s network egress quotas and bursting telemetry. Any best practices?
[07:44] Maya: Reduce synchronous telemetry during hot paths; sample traces, buffer metrics and push on separate thread. Also configure rate-limited prefetch to avoid network saturation during cache fills.
[07:55] Priya: We also saw a case where the orchestration scaled pods too quickly and multiple pods started heavy prefetch at the same time — cluster-scale backpressure would help.
[08:05] Maya: Agreed — use staggered start (randomized backoff) and leader election for initial cache warmup. Also set node-level reservation to limit concurrent prefetchers per node.
[08:20] Samir: Quick check — are there any signs the issue is hardware faults vs software?
[08:25] Priya: We ran diagnostic on a node after a reset and didn't see ECC errors. Most indicators point to fragmentation, allocation surge, and kernel choices.
[08:35] Maya: Ok, we'll prioritize software mitigations first.
[08:40] (Technical deep dive exchange ensues — timestamps every ~30-90s, excerpts shown)
[09:10] Alex: In the sample trace 'trace_20261128_2' we see 3 OOMs in 12 minutes with pattern: short burst, large prefetch, then spike. I'll attach the CSV of batch sizes and seq lengths.
[09:27] Maya: Perfect. We'll run the token-cost model on that CSV, simulate bucketed batching, and output expected peak allocs for a few candidate configs.
[09:36] Jonah: If we change runtime to async eviction, how do we monitor effectiveness?
[09:41] Maya: We'll instrument two new metrics: eviction_spike_rate and async_evict_throughput. Look for elimination of single-step alloc spikes and much lower frequency of CUBLAS_ALLOC failures. We'll also set temporary alert on device_reset_count.
[09:58] Priya: Does Redwood have a recommended throttle algorithm for backpressure when instances approach mem threshold?
[10:04] Maya: Yes — we use token-bucket backpressure with graded shedding: first mark requests as 'degraded' (lower max_out_tokens), then soft-queue for up to X ms, then reject when exceeded. It reduces hard OOMs while keeping p95 stable.
[10:22] Alex: For our ingestion pipeline, we'll add idempotency keys and make downstream ops tolerant of retries.
[10:30] Maya: Great. We'll include a short example header format in the deliverable.
[10:36] Samir: Any blockers for running the stress run this week?
[10:40] Jonah: We need Redwood to confirm the exact stress script and we'll provide credentials in a secure channel. Also we'd like a pre-checklist so we don't trigger production impacts.
[10:50] Maya: We'll share the playbook and a 'noisy neighbor safe' mode that runs at low throttle first.
[10:56] Priya: One more: do you recommend changing pod count vs batch size for throughput? We currently bump concurrent pods to hit throughput which seems to aggravate fragmentation.
[11:05] Maya: Prefer increasing batch size within safe token-budget if latency SLAs allow; adding pods increases total CUDA contexts and can worsen fragmentation if each starts to prefetch large caches. If using cudaMallocAsync and pooled allocators, multiple pods are less harmful.
[11:25] Jonah: Okay. Let's summarize actions and owners.
[11:30] Samir: Recap — Maya to run token-cost sims and provide zipped configs (bucketing, batch caps, env vars). Maya to run a 4-hour stress run with your CSV and post results. Priya to watch device_reset metrics and open support ticket if resets persist. Jonah to provide request histogram and grant access for stress run. Alex to add idempotency headers to critical calls.
[11:54] Maya: Also we will propose an interim runtime config: REDWOOD_EVICTION_MODE=async_with_throttle, MAX_PREFIX_BYTES=0.4, ENABLE_CUDA_MALLOC_ASYNC=1, MAX_BATCH_TOKENS per bucket set to keep peak < 85% memory.
[12:14] Priya: Sounds good. We'll aim to have histogram and traces by Monday.
[12:20] Samir: Perfect — we'll follow up with the playbook and schedule the stress run. Thanks all.

End of transcript.
